summary: One of the documents that together define the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP). This one describes how IPP requests and responses are encoded and carried over HTTP. It is a standards-track document. It was replaced by RFC 8010.

plainLanguage.summary: Printing over a network needs a way to pack up your request and send it. This document says how the package is wrapped and mailed.

questions: how does ipp work over http
subtitle: How IPP print requests are packed into a binary message and carried inside HTTP POST requests.

tldr.problem: The IPP model describes print operations in the abstract. Real clients and printers need an exact byte layout and a transport to exchange them.
tldr.mechanism: Each request or response is a compact binary message of tagged attributes, sent as the body of an HTTP/1.1 POST with the media type application/ipp. A new ipp URL scheme names printers and jobs, with default port 631.
tldr.outcome: This document replaced RFC 2565 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 8010, so it is no longer the current IPP encoding.

today: RFC 2910 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 8010. It was also updated by RFC 3380, RFC 3381, RFC 3382, RFC 3510, RFC 3995 and RFC 7472, so current IPP work should start from the newer document.

sections.title: Two Layers: Operation and Transport
sections.content:
This document is one of a set that together describe the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP). It holds the rules for encoding IPP operations and describes two layers. The transport layer is an HTTP/1.1 request or response. The operation layer is the message body inside that HTTP message.

What an operation means is defined elsewhere, in the Model and Semantics document (RFC 2911). This RFC only says how an operation is written down as bytes and how it travels. The RFC also notes that the IPP version (1.1) and the HTTP version (1.1) are not linked; they just happen to match.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a letter and an envelope. The letter is the print request, and the envelope is HTTP. This document explains both how to write the letter and how to address the envelope.

sections.title: The Operation Layer Encoding
sections.content:
Every request or response carries exactly one IPP operation. It starts with a 2-byte version-number, then a 2-byte operation-id (in a request) or status-code (in a response), then a 4-byte request-id. After that come zero or more attribute groups, a one-byte end-of-attributes-tag, and optional data, such as the document to print.

Integers are signed, two's-complement and big-endian. They are one byte (version and tag fields), two bytes (operation-id, status-code and length fields) or four bytes (values and the request-id). The protocol version is fixed at major 1, minor 1, written %x01.01.

Each attribute group begins with a one-byte delimiter tag, such as 0x01 for operation attributes, 0x02 for job attributes, 0x04 for printer attributes and 0x05 for unsupported attributes. The group ends at the next delimiter tag. The end-of-attributes-tag (0x03) MUST occur exactly once and be the last delimiter.

If an IPP status code is returned, the HTTP status MUST be 200. With any other HTTP status, the response MUST NOT contain an IPP message body.
sections.plainLanguage: A request is a form with the same boxes in the same order every time. First the version, then what you want, then a ticket number, then your details, then a stamp saying the details are done, then the document itself.

sections.title: Attributes, Tags and Value Types
sections.content:
Each attribute is written as a value-tag (one byte), a name-length (two bytes), the name, a value-length (two bytes) and the value. The value tag says what type the value is. For example 0x44 means keyword, 0x21 integer, 0x22 boolean, 0x23 enum and 0x45 uri.

An attribute with several values is written as the first value in full, followed by additional-value fields. An additional value has a name-length of zero, and that zero is the only way the encoding marks a multi-valued attribute. Two attributes with the same name in one group make the group malformed.

Tags below 0x10 are delimiter tags and 0x10 to 0xFF are value tags, so a printer can tell an entire unknown attribute group from a single unknown value. Out-of-band tags such as unsupported (0x10) and no-value (0x13) must have a value length of 0. Tag 0x7F is reserved for extending the tag space beyond 255 values.
sections.plainLanguage: Every fact in the request has a little label saying what kind of fact it is, how long its name is and how long its value is. If a fact has several answers, the extra answers just skip the name.

sections.title: Carrying IPP over HTTP
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 is the transport. A printer MUST support HTTP over port 631, the IANA assigned well known port for IPP, and it may support other ports too. Every HTTP operation MUST use the POST method, with the target object as the request URI and a Content-Type of application/ipp on both requests and responses.

An HTTP server MUST support chunked transfer for IPP requests, and an IPP client MUST support chunking for IPP responses. A server may send a response before it has read the whole request if it detects an error, and it may send an intermediate response such as 100 Continue, so clients must expect both.

The target of an operation appears twice: as the HTTP request URI and as the required printer-uri or job-uri operation attribute. The two need not be identical (one can be relative, the other absolute), but they MUST name the same object, and the one inside the operation MUST be absolute. A printer need not check that they agree.
sections.plainLanguage: The package goes by the normal web mail truck, always as a POST. The street address is written on the outside of the box and again on the letter inside, so both must point to the same printer.

sections.title: The ipp URL Scheme
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new URL scheme, ipp, for printers and jobs. It behaves like http except that it stands for a print service and its default port is 631. Because HTTP does not know the ipp scheme, a client MUST convert the URL before sending: change the scheme to http and add an explicit port 631 if none is present.

The converted http URL goes in the HTTP request line and headers, while the original ipp URL goes in the printer-uri or job-uri attribute inside the body. The RFC's example turns ipp://myhost.com/myprinter/myqueue into a request to port 631 on myhost.com, and shows the same request sent through a proxy on port 8080.

A printer that registers its URL with a directory service MUST register an ipp URL.
sections.plainLanguage: An ipp address is a web address with a printer sticker on it. Before mailing, you peel off the sticker and use the normal web address, but you keep the sticker address written inside the letter.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC builds on three needs from the Model document: client authentication, server authentication and operation privacy. IPP clients MUST support HTTP Digest Authentication, including MD5 and MD5-sess, while printers SHOULD support it. The RFC explains the weaker requirement for printers: a low-end device with limited ROM may not need client authentication, while a high-volume device is prone to losing consumables and paper to unauthorized use.

Printers SHOULD support TLS for server authentication and operation privacy, and MAY use it for client authentication. Any implementation that supports TLS MUST support the cipher suite TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA. IPP uses the HTTP upgrade mechanism of RFC 2817, so an initial request never uses TLS. For backward compatibility with IPP/1.0, SSL3 may also be supported.

Security MUST NOT be weakened when a client sends a lower version number or a non-secure URL scheme. A printer that enforces Digest Authentication for version 1.1 must enforce it for version 1.0 too.
sections.plainLanguage: Big busy printers should ask who you are, like a guard checking badges. Everyone should be able to whisper to the printer in a secret code (TLS). Sending an older-style request must never be a way to sneak past the guard.
